set1.io: Describe the antigens’ ability to promote an immune response
set1.q: What starts the antigen-dependent phase of B-cell maturation?
opts: Correct. The antigen-dependent phase, in which the B cell differentiates into a plasma cell making specific antibody, is initiated by exposure to the antigen.
Surface IgM is expressed in the earlier, antigen-INDEPENDENT phase of maturation.
Perforin release belongs to cytotoxic T cells killing their targets, not to B-cell maturation.
Thymic processing is how T lymphocytes mature; B cells mature in the bone marrow.

set1.io: Compare and contrast the various types of blood cells and their roles in immunity
set1.q: Which surface marker identifies natural killer cells?
opts: CD3 marks T cells, with CD4 or CD8 on the major subsets; natural killer cells carry CD56 instead.
CD4 marks helper T cells, which recognize peptides on major histocompatibility complex class II molecules.
CD19 and CD20 are found on many B cells, so this marker points to a B lymphocyte rather than the cell asked about.
Correct. Natural killer cells carry CD56, and many also carry CD16, which binds the Fc region of IgG.

set1.io: Compare and contrast the various types of blood cells and their roles in immunity
set1.q: Which form immediately precedes the segmented neutrophil?
opts: The metamyelocyte comes one step earlier; it matures into the band form, which then becomes the segmented neutrophil.
The myelocyte is two steps earlier: myelocyte, metamyelocyte, band, then segmented neutrophil.
The monoblast belongs to a different line, ending in the monocyte rather than the neutrophil.
Correct. The neutrophil line runs promyelocyte, myelocyte, metamyelocyte, then the band form, then the segmented neutrophil.

set1.io: Compare and contrast the functions of the various types of antibodies and the various mechanisms by which antibodies destroy antigens
set1.q: Which immunoglobulin binds mast cells and basophils?
opts: IgD is part of the receptor system on many mature naive B cells.
IgA works at mucosal surfaces, preventing microbial attachment.
IgM agglutinates and efficiently activates classical complement.
Correct. IgE binds mast cells and basophils through high-affinity receptors and contributes to allergy and parasite defense.

set1.io: Compare and contrast the various mechanisms that T lymphocytes destroy antigens
set1.q: How do cytotoxic T cells kill infected cells?
opts: Correct. Perforin release is important to the effector function, and perforin with granzymes helps trigger target-cell apoptosis.
Osmotic lysis through assembled pores is the complement membrane attack complex, not T-cell killing.
Coating a target for ingestion is opsonization by antibody or complement.
Blocking attachment or entry is antibody neutralization, which works outside the cell.

set1.io: Compare and contrast the functions of the various types of antibodies and the various mechanisms by which antibodies destroy antigens
set1.q: How do antibodies bring about lysis of a target cell?
opts: Correct. Lysis, destruction of the cell, happens through incorporation with the complement system.
Perforin is released by cytotoxic T cells and natural killer cells, not by antibodies.
Cross-linking soluble antigen produces precipitation, not lysis.
By coating the cell for phagocytes
Coating for phagocytes is opsonization, which leads to ingestion rather than lysis.

set1.io: Describe the function of the complement system
set1.q: Which complement fragment coats targets as an opsonin?
opts: C5a promotes the inflammatory response, attracting phagocytes; it does not coat targets.
Correct. C3b coats the target for opsonization by macrophages, while C3a, C4a and C5a promote the inflammatory response.
C3a is the small fragment that promotes inflammation, such as histamine release.
C9 subunits form the membrane attack complex channel, causing lysis.

set1.io: Define the function and specific types of antigens
set1.q: What does an adaptive B-cell or T-cell receptor recognize?
opts: Patterns shared by groups of organisms
That describes innate receptors, which recognize patterns shared by groups of organisms rather than one epitope.
Correct. Adaptive specificity means B-cell and T-cell receptors recognize particular epitopes, the specific regions of an antigen.
Any foreign protein, whatever its shape
Adaptive receptors are specific: each recognizes a particular epitope, not any foreign protein.
Antigens met in a previous exposure
Recognition does not require prior exposure; memory only makes the response faster and stronger on re-exposure.

set1.io: Describe T-lymphocytes
set1.q: Which surface marker is found on T cells as a group?
opts: Correct. T cells carry CD3, with CD4 or CD8 on the major subsets.
CD4 marks helper T cells and many regulatory T cells, not all T cells; CD3 is the marker across T cells.
CD8 marks only the cytotoxic subset; CD3 is the marker across T cells.
CD19 and CD20 are found on many B cells, so this marker points to a B lymphocyte rather than the cell asked about.

set1.io: Describe the effect of aging on the immune system
set1.q: How do changes in older adults affect immune responses?
opts: That reverses it: lymphocyte changes with age reduce responses to new antigens.
Correct. In older adults, changes in lymphocyte function and repertoire can reduce responses to new antigens, and autoantibodies become more common.
Autoantibodies become MORE common with age; clinical findings determine their significance.
Maternal IgG protects neonates and declines in infancy; it has no role in old age.

set1.io: Compare and contrast examples of autoimmune diseases
set1.q: Lupus is an example of which hypersensitivity type?
opts: Type I is IgE- and mast cell-mediated allergy and anaphylaxis.
Type II examples are ABO incompatibility and anti-glomerular basement membrane disease.
Correct. Lupus is a type III immune-complex example, alongside immune-complex glomerulonephritis or arthritis.
Type IV examples are contact dermatitis, tuberculosis-related reactions and transplant rejection.

set1.io: Compare and contrast primary and secondary immunodeficiency including the genetic basis
set1.q: What distinguishes primary from secondary immunodeficiency?
opts: Medications cause SECONDARY immunodeficiency, an acquired defect.
Malignancy is a cause of secondary immunodeficiency; primary defects are intrinsic.
Inadequate nutrition is an acquired, secondary cause; primary defects are intrinsic and often genetic.

Correct. Primary immunodeficiency is an intrinsic defect in immune development or function, often with a genetic basis; secondary immunodeficiency is reduced function from disease, medications, malignancy or inadequate nutrition.

set1.io: Compare and contrast the functions of the various types of antibodies and the various mechanisms by which antibodies destroy antigens
set1.q: Why is IgM especially effective at agglutination?
opts: Crossing the placenta is an IgG property and has nothing to do with clumping particles.
Correct. Secreted IgM is usually a pentamer that places many binding sites around one molecule, so it links antigen-bearing particles into clumps; agglutination is one of its main functions.
Binding high-affinity receptors on mast cells and basophils is IgE.
The secretory component belongs to secretory IgA, a dimer, which works at mucosal surfaces.

set1.io: Compare and contrast the morphology of the various types of antibodies
set1.q: Approximately what share of serum immunoglobulin is IgG?
opts: Less than 1% is the share of IgD and of IgE; IgG is the most abundant class, at 75–80%.
5–10% is the approximate share of IgM; IgG makes up about 75–80% of serum immunoglobulin.
10–15% is the approximate share of IgA; IgG makes up about 75–80% of serum immunoglobulin.
Correct. IgG is the most abundant class, approximately 75–80% of serum immunoglobulin (700–1700 mg/dL); reference intervals vary by laboratory.

set1.io: Compare and contrast primary and secondary immune response by the body
set1.q: How does the secondary response differ from the primary response?
opts: Correct. Memory cells support a generally faster and stronger response on re-exposure, and class-switched antibodies, often IgG, may reach higher levels and persist longer.
That reverses it: IgM leads the primary response, and the secondary response is faster.
Same speed but with more IgE
The secondary response is faster, and the class that rises is often IgG.
Memory cells formed in the primary response are exactly what make the secondary response faster.

set1.io: Compare and contrast the types of hypersensitivity reactions
set1.q: Which of these is a T-cell-mediated hypersensitivity reaction?
opts: Anaphylaxis is type I, mediated by IgE on mast cells; insect venoms are one trigger.
ABO incompatibility is type II, antibody against red-cell antigens.
Serum sickness is type III, a systemic reaction to circulating immune complexes.
Correct. Contact dermatitis is type IV, mediated by sensitized CD4 or CD8 T cells, along with tuberculosis-related reactions and T-cell-mediated transplant rejection.

set1.io: Compare and contrast the morphology of the various types of antibodies
set1.q: What forms the antigen-binding site of an antibody?
opts: The light-chain constant region sits in the arm but does not form the binding site.
The heavy-chain constant region determines class and, in the Fc, effector functions.
Heavy and light variable regions together
Correct. Heavy- and light-chain variable regions jointly form the antigen-binding site at the tip of each arm.
The hinge lies where the arms meet the stem; binding happens at the variable regions at the arm tips.

set1.io: Describe the function of the complement system
set1.q: How does the membrane attack complex kill a target cell?
opts: Granzyme-triggered apoptosis is the cytotoxic T cell's mechanism.
It disrupts ionic and osmotic balance
Correct. The pores damage the membrane and disrupt ionic and osmotic balance; ions and water move abnormally, and severe disruption leads to cell lysis.
It coats the cell for phagocytes
Coating for phagocytes is opsonization, done by C3b rather than the terminal complex.
It blocks the cell's receptor binding
Blocking an essential interaction is antibody neutralization.

set1.io: Describe T-lymphocytes
set1.q: Helper T cells recognize antigenic peptides presented on which molecules?
opts: Correct. Helper (CD4) T cells recognize antigenic peptides presented by major histocompatibility complex class II molecules.
Class I presents peptides to CD8 cytotoxic T cells; helper (CD4) T cells need class II.
Surface immunoglobulin is the B cell's own antigen receptor, not the molecule that presents peptide to helper T cells.
CD16 on natural killer cells binds the Fc region of IgG; it does not present peptide.

set1.io: Compare and contrast the functions of the various types of antibodies and the various mechanisms by which antibodies destroy antigens
set1.q: How does neutralization protect without destroying the target?
opts: It clumps the targets into lattices
Clumping antigen-bearing particles is agglutination; neutralization blocks an interaction and leaves the target intact.
It coats the targets for phagocytes
Coating to ease ingestion is opsonization, which leads to the target being engulfed.
It blocks an essential host interaction
Correct. Antibody binding blocks an essential interaction with a host cell, preventing viral attachment or entry or a toxin reaching its target, and limits activity without physical destruction.
It assembles pores in their membranes
Pore assembly is the complement membrane attack complex, which does destroy the target by lysis.

set1.io: Compare and contrast natural and artificial immunity
set1.q: What makes vaccination a form of ARTIFICIAL active immunity?
opts: Receiving preformed antibodies from another source is passive immunity, such as tetanus or rabies immune globulin.
The antigen is met through ordinary contact
Contact with the antigen in the ordinary course of life makes active immunity natural rather than artificial.
Antigen exposure is done on purpose
Correct. Active immunity is acquired by the body's own processes after exposure to the antigen; it is artificial when the exposure is deliberate, as with vaccination.
It acts with no prior sensitization
Defenses that act without prior sensitization are innate. Vaccination works by sensitizing the body to the antigen.

set1.io: Compare and contrast the functions of the various types of antibodies and the various mechanisms by which antibodies destroy antigens
set1.q: What is precipitation, as an antibody function?
opts: Clumping cells or particles that carry surface antigen is agglutination.
A coating that eases ingestion by phagocytes is opsonization, not precipitation of soluble antigen.
Correct. Antibodies cross-link soluble antigens into larger complexes that can become insoluble and precipitate, which may help phagocytes clear them.
Blocking viral attachment or entry is neutralization; precipitation cross-links soluble antigen.

set1.io: Compare and contrast the various types of blood cells and their roles in immunity
set1.q: Which leukocyte is the most numerous first responder, acting by phagocytosis?
opts: Eosinophils are linked with allergic reactions and parasitic invasion, not the first-responder role.
Basophils are similar to tissue mast cells and much less numerous than neutrophils.
Correct. Neutrophils, the “poly” or PMN (polymorphonuclear leukocyte), are the most numerous first responders and act by phagocytosis.
Monocytes are agranulocytes that enter tissue and become macrophages; the most numerous first responder is the neutrophil.

set1.io: Describe the function of the complement system
set1.q: Which organ produces many of the circulating complement components?
opts: Bone marrow produces blood cells and is where B cells mature, not the main source of complement proteins.
The thymus is where T lymphocytes are processed, not the main source of complement proteins (the liver).
The spleen is a peripheral lymphoid organ; the complement proteins come mainly from the liver.
Correct. The liver produces many circulating complement components, and many circulate as inactive precursors until activation starts a regulated cascade.

set1.io: Describe the molecular mechanisms involved in immune processes
set1.q: How does interstitial fluid enter a lymphatic capillary?
opts: Correct. The capillary wall is built of overlapping endothelial cells whose edges act as valves: they open to let interstitial fluid in and close behind it, so flow runs one way.
Through smooth muscle pores in the wall
Fluid does not pass through pores in a muscle layer; it enters between overlapping endothelial cells, whose edges open like one-way valves.
By active pumping across a basement membrane
No pump moves fluid in. Interstitial fluid flows in passively where the overlapping endothelial edges part, which work like one-way valves.
Driven in by the heart's systolic pressure
The heart does not drive lymph. Fluid enters between overlapping endothelial cells, and outside forces such as muscle movement keep lymph moving.

set1.io: Compare and contrast the various types of blood cells and their roles in immunity
set1.q: What does a monocyte become once it enters tissue during inflammation?
opts: Plasma cells come from B lymphocytes and produce antibodies; monocytes become macrophages.
Correct. Monocytes circulate in blood and enter tissues during inflammation, where tissue signals promote differentiation into macrophages.
Mast cells are the tissue cells basophils resemble; a monocyte entering tissue becomes a macrophage.
Neutrophils are granulocytes that mature through the band form; a monocyte that enters tissue becomes a macrophage.

set1.io: Compare and contrast the types of hypersensitivity reactions
set1.q: The Arthus reaction and serum sickness are examples of which hypersensitivity type?
opts: Type I is IgE-mediated immediate hypersensitivity, as in anaphylaxis.
Type II is antibody bound to fixed cell or tissue antigens, as in ABO incompatibility.

Correct. Both are type III immune-complex reactions: the Arthus reaction is a local response in a previously sensitized person, and serum sickness is a systemic reaction to circulating immune complexes.
Type IV is T-cell-mediated, as in contact dermatitis; the Arthus reaction and serum sickness are type III.

set1.io: Compare and contrast the morphology of the various types of antibodies
set1.q: What determines an immunoglobulin's class?
opts: Whether the light chain is kappa or lambda
Every class can carry kappa or lambda light chains; class is set by the heavy chain.
Correct. The heavy-chain constant region determines immunoglobulin class (heavy chain mu, delta, gamma, epsilon or alpha).
Variable regions decide WHAT the antibody binds, not its class.
Disulfide bonds connect chains and support structure; they do not define class.

set1.io: Describe the molecular mechanisms involved in immune processes
set1.q: Which step follows adherence of the microbe to the phagocyte?
opts: Correct. The sequence is: the microbe adheres; pseudopods engulf it into a phagosome; the phagosome fuses with a lysosome; enzymes digest it; residual material leaves by exocytosis.
Fusion with a lysosome comes after engulfment, once a phagosome has formed.
Exocytosis of indigestible residue is the final step, after digestion in the phagolysosome.
Digestion by lysosomal acid hydrolases happens later, inside the phagolysosome.

set1.io: Compare and contrast natural and artificial immunity
set1.q: Which is an example of NATURAL passive immunity?
opts: Rabies immune globulin given after exposure
Rabies and tetanus immune globulin are ARTIFICIAL passive immunity: preformed antibodies given on purpose.
Correct. Natural passive immunity is maternal IgG through the placenta and IgA in breast milk: preformed antibodies from another source, transferred naturally.
Antibodies made after a natural infection
Making your own antibodies after contact with the antigen is natural ACTIVE immunity, not passive.
A vaccine series that builds antibody
A vaccine is artificial active immunity: the body makes its own response to an antigen given on purpose.

set2.io: Compare and contrast the functions of the various types of antibodies and the various mechanisms by which antibodies destroy antigens
set2.q: Which antibodies are usually present in the plasma of a group O person?
opts: Anti-A without anti-B is the usual plasma pattern of group B, whose red cells carry B.
Anti-B without anti-A is the usual plasma pattern of group A, whose red cells carry A.
Lacking both antibodies is group AB, whose red cells carry both A and B.
Correct. Group O red cells carry neither A nor B antigen, and group O plasma usually carries both anti-A and anti-B.

set2.io: Describe the molecular mechanisms involved in immune processes
set2.q: Which function of immunity removes cellular debris?
opts: Correct. Immunity is a state of protection with three functions: defense (resistance to invaders), surveillance (of self for mutant or cancerous cells) and homeostasis (removing cellular debris).
Defense is resistance to invaders. Clearing cellular debris is the homeostasis function of immunity.
Surveillance watches the body's own cells for mutant or cancerous change. Removing cellular debris is homeostasis.
Memory is a faster, stronger adaptive response on re-exposure to an antigen, not one of the three functions; debris removal is homeostasis.

set2.io: Compare and contrast the types of hypersensitivity reactions
set2.q: Which mechanism defines type II hypersensitivity?
opts: IgE fixed on mast cells defines type I; type II is IgG or IgM bound to cell or tissue antigen.
Antigen–antibody complexes depositing in tissues or vessel walls define type III.
IgG or IgM binding cell or tissue antigens
Correct. In type II hypersensitivity IgG or IgM binds antigens on cells or within tissues, and injury follows through phagocytosis, complement or antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity.
Sensitized T cells mediate type IV; type II is antibody (IgG or IgM) bound to cell or tissue antigen.

set2.io: Describe the molecular mechanisms involved in immune processes
set2.q: What keeps lymph moving along the larger lymphatic vessels?
opts: Lymph has no central pump. It is propelled by skeletal muscle movement, breathing-related pressure changes and the pulsation of nearby arteries.
Gravity draining it down toward the feet
That reverses the direction: lymph returns toward the circulation, and physical activity or passive movement keeps it flowing at a decent pace.
Muscle movement, breathing and arterial pulsation
Correct. Skeletal muscle movement, pressure changes in the thorax during breathing and the pulsations of adjacent arteries help propel lymph, while the vessel's valves keep it moving forward.
Cilia beating along the lymphatic lumen
No cilia line the lymphatic vessel. Its internal valves keep lymph moving forward, and outside forces such as muscle movement push it along.

set2.io: Describe the molecular mechanisms involved in immune processes
set2.q: What forms when the vesicle holding an engulfed microbe fuses with a lysosome?
opts: Correct. The phagocytic vesicle (phagosome) fuses with a lysosome to form the phagolysosome, where lysosomal enzymes kill and digest the microbe.
The residual body is what is left AFTER digestion in the phagolysosome; it is removed by exocytosis.
Pseudopods are the extensions that engulf the particle at the start, before any fusion.
The membrane attack complex is a complement pore in a target membrane, not a phagocytic compartment.

set2.io: Compare and contrast the various types of blood cells and their roles in immunity
set2.q: From which precursor do lymphocytes arise?
opts: The myeloblast is a granulocyte precursor, giving the eosinophil and the basophil; lymphocytes come from the lymphoblast.
The monoblast gives rise to the monocyte, the other agranulocyte, not the lymphocyte.
Correct. In blood cell formation the hematopoietic stem cell gives rise to the lymphoblast, which becomes the lymphocyte.
The megakaryocyte, from the promegakaryocyte, sheds platelets; it plays no part in making lymphocytes.

set2.io: Define the concept of hypersensitivity
set2.q: What defines hypersensitivity?
opts: Any immune response to a foreign antigen
Most immune responses protect without injury; hypersensitivity is the subset that harms the body.
Too little immune function is immunodeficiency, such as X-linked agammaglobulinemia.
Immune reactions that injure the body
Correct. Hypersensitivity is when immune reactions, either humoral or cellular, result in injury to the body; four types are seen.
Infection is the threat itself; hypersensitivity is injury caused by the immune reaction.

set2.io: Compare and contrast the various types of blood cells and their roles in immunity
set2.q: Which cell, when seen on a stained smear, is NOT a normal constituent of peripheral blood?
opts: Monocytes circulate normally in blood before entering tissue as macrophages.
ruled out by a stated finding
Small lymphocytes are normal circulating agranulocytes, shown alongside medium lymphocytes on the smear.
ruled out by a stated finding
Correct. A plasma cell is not a normal constituent of peripheral blood; it is shown beside the nongranular leukocytes for comparison.
Eosinophils are normal circulating granulocytes, shown on the smear beside neutrophils and basophils.
ruled out by a stated finding

set2.io: Compare and contrast the functions of the various types of antibodies and the various mechanisms by which antibodies destroy antigens
set2.q: Which immunoglobulin crosses the placenta?
opts: IgM is usually secreted as a pentamer and is often the first class in a new response; it does not cross the placenta.
Correct. IgG crosses the placenta and provides maternal protection; it is also the most abundant serum class.
IgA protects mucosal surfaces and reaches the infant in breast milk, not across the placenta.
IgE binds mast cells and basophils in allergy and parasite defense.

set2.io: Compare and contrast the functions of the various types of antibodies and the various mechanisms by which antibodies destroy antigens
set2.q: Which pair of antibody effects acts on a soluble toxin?
opts: Opsonization and lysis act on cells such as bacteria, whose surfaces carry antigenic determinants.
Agglutination needs antigen on particles or cells; a soluble toxin has no surface to clump.
ruled out by a stated finding
Both need a cell or particle surface; a soluble toxin is neutralized and precipitated instead.
ruled out by a stated finding
Correct. A toxin is soluble, so antibodies neutralize its action and cross-link toxin molecules into precipitating complexes; viruses are neutralized and agglutinated, bacteria opsonized.

set2.io: Describe the function of the complement system
set2.q: Which components assemble the membrane attack complex?
opts: Correct. C5b initiates assembly of the terminal components C6–C9, and the assembled complex forms pores in a susceptible target membrane.
C1, C4 and C2 begin the classical pathway, far upstream of the attack complex.
C3a and C5a are released fragments that promote inflammation.
Factor B and factor D act in the alternative pathway to form a C3 convertase.

set2.io: Compare and contrast primary and secondary immunodeficiency including the genetic basis
set2.q: Which defect underlies X-linked agammaglobulinemia?
opts: Variable impairment of thymic and T-cell development is DiGeorge syndrome.
Profound T-cell dysfunction with impaired B-cell immunity is severe combined immunodeficiency.
Reduced function from medications is secondary immunodeficiency; X-linked agammaglobulinemia is primary, with a genetic basis.
Correct. X-linked agammaglobulinemia is impaired B-cell maturation with very low antibodies, and is associated with recurrent pyogenic bacterial infections.

set2.io: Compare and contrast the various types of immunological processes
set2.q: Which of these organs belongs to the lymphatic system?
opts: The thyroid sits in the neck near the thymus but is not among the lymphatic structures labeled; the thymus is the lymphoid organ there, where T cells are processed.
Correct. The labeled lymphatic system includes the thymus gland together with the tonsils, spleen, appendix, lymph vessels and the lymph nodes of the neck, axilla, groin and knee.
The adrenal gland is not part of the lymphatic network. The lymphoid organs labeled in the abdomen are the spleen and the appendix.
The pancreas is not a lymphoid organ. The lymphatic system's organs are the tonsils, thymus, spleen and appendix, joined by vessels and nodes.

set2.io: Compare and contrast the types of hypersensitivity reactions
set2.q: Which hypersensitivity type is mediated by IgE fixed on mast cells?
opts: Correct. Type I (anaphylactic, immediate) hypersensitivity: IgE made at a first exposure becomes fixed on mast cells and basophils, and re-exposure releases histamine and other substances.
Type II is antibody-mediated through IgG or IgM binding antigens on cells or within tissues.
Type III is immune-complex hypersensitivity: antigen–antibody complexes deposit in tissues or vessel walls.
Type IV is mediated by sensitized CD4 or CD8 T cells, not by antibody.

set2.io: Describe the function of the complement system
set2.q: What commonly starts the classical complement pathway?
opts: Recognition proteins binding microbial carbohydrates start the lectin pathway.
C1 binding antigen-bound IgM or IgG
Correct. The classical pathway commonly begins when C1 recognizes antigen-bound IgM or IgG, though some activation occurs without antibody.
C3 activation and amplification on permissive surfaces is the alternative pathway.
C5b starts the terminal membrane attack complex, the shared END of the pathways.

set2.io: Define autoimmunity
set2.q: Which T cells limit immune activation and maintain self-tolerance?
opts: Cytotoxic T cells kill infected or malignant host cells; they do not restrain the response.
Helper T cells coordinate and support responses; the restraining population is the regulatory T cell.
Memory T cells carry forward a faster response on re-exposure; they do not maintain self-tolerance.
Correct. Regulatory T cells limit immune activation and maintain self-tolerance; many are CD4 cells expressing FOXP3.

set2.io: Compare and contrast primary and secondary immune response by the body
set2.q: After a FIRST exposure to an antigen, which antibody class rises first?
opts: IgG starts rising later than IgM in the primary response; it dominates the secondary response.
IgA is the mucosal class; the first class to rise after a first exposure is IgM.
Correct. On the primary response time course IgM rises and peaks first, and IgG starts later; on second exposure IgG dominates.
IgE binds mast cells and basophils in allergy; it is not the early class of the primary response.

set2.io: Compare and contrast the morphology of the various types of antibodies
set2.q: What makes up a basic antibody unit?
opts: One heavy and one light chain
That is only half a unit, the pairing found within one arm of the Y.
The unit has two heavy chains and two light chains, not four heavy chains.
Light chains are part of every basic unit; each arm pairs a light chain with a heavy chain.
Two heavy and two light chains
Correct. A basic antibody unit has two heavy chains and two light chains, connected by disulfide bonds.

set2.io: Compare and contrast the various subtypes and various functions of T lymphocytes
set2.q: What is the main role of CD4 helper T cells?
opts: Perforin killing is the work of CD8 cytotoxic T cells; helpers coordinate rather than kill.
Correct. CD4 helper T cells coordinate cell-mediated and humoral responses, using cytokines and cell contact to regulate other immune populations.
Plasma cells secrete antibodies; helper signals support their differentiation.
Limiting immune activation and maintaining self-tolerance is the role of regulatory T cells.

set2.io: Compare and contrast the morphology of the various types of antibodies
set2.q: Which immunoglobulin is usually secreted as a pentamer?
opts: Secretory IgA is usually a dimer with a J chain and secretory component.
Correct. IgM is usually secreted as a pentamer with a J chain, and is a monomer on the B-cell surface.
IgG is a monomer with four subclasses; the pentamer secreted in a new response is IgM.
IgD is a monomer found with IgM on many mature naive B cells.

set2.io: Describe B lymphocyte and its metamorphosis into plasma cells
set2.q: Which cells actually produce antibodies?
opts: Correct. In humoral immunity B cells are transformed into plasma cells, which are the actual antibody-producing cells.
Naive B cells carry antibody on their surface as a receptor but must become plasma cells to secrete it.
Helper T cells support B-cell differentiation and antibody production, but plasma cells do the secreting.
Memory B cells wait to respond to a later exposure; the antibody-secreting cell is the plasma cell.

set2.io: Compare and contrast acquired and innate immunity
set2.q: Which defenses belong to innate immunity?
opts: Correct. Innate immunity acts without prior sensitization and includes skin and mucosal barriers, phagocytes, complement and interferons, with natural killer cells as its cytotoxic defense.
Memory B cells from a past exposure
Memory cells are adaptive: they exist only because of an earlier exposure, the opposite of innate defense.
Antibodies left by a past vaccine
Antibodies made after a vaccine are artificial active immunity, which is adaptive and needs sensitization.
Cytotoxic T cells with specific receptors
Antigen-specific T-cell receptors are adaptive. The innate cytotoxic defense is the natural killer cell.

set2.io: Compare and contrast the various types of blood cells and their roles in immunity
set2.q: Besides circulating monocytes, what is another origin of resident tissue macrophages?
opts: Neutrophils are the first-responder granulocytes that act by phagocytosis; they never become macrophages, which come from monocytes or develop before birth.
The thymus processes T lymphocytes; macrophages come from monocytes, or develop before birth and renew locally.
Development before birth, then local renewal
Correct. Monocytes enter tissue during inflammation and become macrophages, but some resident macrophages develop before birth and renew locally.
B cells changing after antigen exposure
B cells become plasma cells and memory cells after antigen exposure, never macrophages.

set2.io: Compare and contrast the various subtypes and various functions of T lymphocytes
set2.q: How do natural killer cells differ from cytotoxic T cells?
opts: Thymic processing is the T-cell route. Natural killer cells mature in bone marrow and other tissues.
Antibodies come from plasma cells. Natural killer cells kill with perforin and granzymes.
Correct. Unlike cytotoxic T cells, natural killer cells do not need to recognize a specific antigen; they target tumor cells and protect against many infectious microbes.
They need a prior exposure first
Natural killer cells are innate and act without prior sensitization; they keep no conventional memory.

set2.io: Compare and contrast primary and secondary immunodeficiency including the genetic basis
set2.q: Why is severe combined immunodeficiency called combined?
opts: T-cell and B-cell immunity both fail
Correct. Severe combined immunodeficiency is profound T-cell dysfunction with impaired B-cell immunity; it may present in early infancy or be found by newborn screening.
It combines primary and secondary causes
It is a primary immunodeficiency; secondary causes are acquired from disease, medications, malignancy or nutrition.
It affects both complement and antibody
The combination is cellular and humoral: profound T-cell dysfunction plus impaired B-cell immunity.
It joins allergy with immune deficiency
Allergy is type I hypersensitivity; this disorder is a combined T-cell and B-cell deficiency.

set2.io: Compare and contrast the functions of the various types of antibodies and the various mechanisms by which antibodies destroy antigens
set2.q: What is opsonization?
opts: Clumping of particles into a lattice
Clumping particles together is agglutination; opsonization coats a target so a phagocyte ingests it.
Pore formation in a target membrane
Pore formation is the complement membrane attack complex leading to lysis.
Blocking a toxin from its target
Blocking a toxin's action is neutralization; opsonization is a coating that eases phagocyte ingestion.
Coating that eases ingestion by phagocytes
Correct. In opsonization antibody joins antigen on the cell's surface, and this coating facilitates ingestion of the antigen by a phagocyte.

set2.io: Define antibodies (immunoglobulins)
set2.q: What does immunofixation add to serum protein electrophoresis?
opts: Correct. Electrophoresis separates serum proteins into albumin and globulin fractions by migration in an electric field; immunofixation characterizes the immunoglobulin heavy- and light-chain types.
Separating albumin and globulin fractions is what electrophoresis itself does.
Immunofixation characterizes immunoglobulins, not the complement cascade.
A count of CD4 helper T cells
Lymphocyte populations are counted by their surface markers, not by protein electrophoresis.

set2.io: Describe the process known as cellular immunity
set2.q: Why does impaired helper T-cell function weaken antibody responses?
opts: Helper T cells secrete the antibodies
Plasma cells secrete antibodies; the helper cell's contribution is the supporting signal.
Helper T cells form the B-cell receptor
The B-cell antigen receptor is surface immunoglobulin made by the B cell itself.
Helper T cells carry antibody to tissue
Antibodies travel in blood, tissue fluid and secretions on their own; helper cells act through cytokines and contact.
Correct. Helper signals support B-cell differentiation and antibody production, so losing them weakens the antibody response even though plasma cells do the secreting.

set2.io: Compare and contrast the functions of the various types of antibodies and the various mechanisms by which antibodies destroy antigens
set2.q: Which antibody fragment carries the effector functions?
opts: Fab contains the antigen-binding regions and adjacent constant domains, not the effector region.
Correct. Fc contains the heavy-chain constant regions involved in effector functions; the complement-binding site lies on its CH2 domain.
The light-chain variable region helps form the antigen-binding site, which is binding, not effector function.
The hinge joins the arms to the stem; the effector functions sit in the Fc.

set2.io: Describe the function of the complement system
set2.q: Which three main functions does complement serve?
opts: Antibody secretion is the plasma cell's work and memory belongs to lymphocytes; only opsonization is a complement function.

Correct. Complement opsonizes targets for phagocytes, generates inflammatory mediators that recruit and activate immune cells, and forms the membrane attack complex that damages susceptible membranes.
Antigen presentation and memory are lymphocyte and antigen-presenting cell functions.
These are antibody functions; complement adds opsonization, inflammation and membrane attack.
